Article Title: OpenAI chief scientist reveals one metric that could predict AI's next big leap; says 2027 could be crucial
Article Text:
OpenAI chief scientist reveals one metric that could predict AI's next big leap; says 2027 could be crucial

Here’s the blog post shared by OpenAI chief scientist

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities.

There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI.

In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry.

We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model.

Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions.

The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task.

GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT.

GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.

I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4.

In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight.

Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial.

There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them.

Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.

Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too.

While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today.

At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards.

I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it.

I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

Article Title: AI godfather Yann LeCun accuses Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei of wanting open AI models banned; says: It stops the population from...
Article Text:
Yann LeCun says Dario Amodei wants open AI models banned

LeCun says Amodei has pushed the same line since GPT-2

Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei say they have never asked for a ban on open models

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Turing Award winner Yann LeCun has accused Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei of spending years talking up the dangers of AI so that open models would be made illegal and Anthropic would stay in charge. In a post on X, the former Meta chief AI scientist compared Amodei's stance to the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic to keep control of religious dogma. "It stops the population from freely accessing diverse knowledge," LeCun wrote, calling it "a new form of medieval obscurantism."LeCun was responding to a video of Amodei that has been doing the rounds on X. In it, Amodei tells US lawmakers that open-source AI is heading down a "very dangerous path". His reasoning is simple. A company that runs a closed model can watch how it is used, cut off bad actors and update its safeguards. A model released in the open can never be pulled back.The clip, however, is old. It comes from Amodei's testimony before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee in July 2023, but it is being shared as fresh, with captions claiming he believes the most advanced AI should not be put in everyone's hands."Dario's spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal and he would stay in control," LeCun wrote. He also claimed Amodei left OpenAI "because he wasn't going to have control."The GPT-2 reference goes back to 2019, when OpenAI held back the full version of that model over misuse fears. Amodei was the company's vice president of research at the time. He left OpenAI in 2020 with a group of colleagues over disagreements on how to build AI safely, and they founded Anthropic the following year.LeCun has his own stake in the open camp. He left Meta after 12 years to found AMI Labs, a Paris-headquartered startup with more than 60 employees that builds world models for industrial uses, such as spotting a failing machine on a factory floor. He has said its first product is coming soon and may involve open models.This is also not his first swipe at Amodei. In an interview in October, LeCun called the Anthropic CEO "deluded" and "crazy", described the effective altruism movement as "super toxic", and said he worries far more about regulatory capture than about AI wiping out humanity. Oddly, he also called Amodei "honest", saying he was doing what was best for a company nearing its IPO. Anthropic made its stock market debut last week.Amodei has already answered this exact charge. In a blog post in July, he wrote, "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models." He described open models that lack dangerous capabilities as "a public good" that costs nothing beyond the compute needed to run them.His post followed a busy July. OpenAI's agents had gone rogue and hacked Hugging Face, an incident LeCun later blamed on sandboxes that were "leaky and horribly designed". Soon after, as Washington weighed curbs on Chinese open models, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Microsoft's Satya Nadella drove an industry letter backing open-weights models. More than 200 companies, including OpenAI, eventually signed it.Amodei refused. He said he disagreed with the letter's claim that open models make safeguards easier to build. Open weights are harder to put guardrails on or monitor, he argued, and "once weights are released they cannot be withdrawn". In place of a ban, he has called for three measures: no sales of advanced chips to China, a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation of US models, and mandatory safety testing for every sufficiently capable model, whether open or closed.Huang has since lost his seat at the top of Nvidia. He stepped down as CEO earlier this month under pressure from the company's board, after steering the chipmaker towards a $26 billion investment in open models over five years and a $12.9 billion deal to buy Hugging Face.
Article Summary: Yann LeCun says Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants open-source AI banned. He compares his stance to the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic. Anthropic and its CEO say they have never asked for a ban on open models.

Article Title: Amazon is showing a 'special message' to its customers in New York on its app; and it's a 'warning' about their mayor Zohran Mamdani
Article Text:
Amazon ask customers to contact lawmakers

What is New York City's Delivery Protection Act

Mamdani fires back

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

City Council rejects Amazon's claims

Amazon has recently launched an unusual in-app website campaign against New York City shoppers, warning that a proposed law backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani could lead to an increase in delivery costs by as much as $5 per order asking customers to lobby local lawmakers against the measure. According to a report by Wall Street Journal, New Yorkers when opening Amazon app or listing its website were greeted with a message reading, “NYC Council Could add up to $5 per order. ” The message refers to the Delivery Protection Act, also known as Intro 518, a bill supported by Mamdani that would impose new licensing, safety, training and employment requirements on warehouse operators such as Amazon.The e-commerce major is not on displaying warning messages but it is also redirecting customers to a form which enables them to send pre-written emails to their City Council representatives opposing the legislation. As per the WSJ report, the template message emphasises that the bill could lead to increase in annual delivery costs for New Yorkers and also worsen the affordability pressures. An Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said that the company wanted to be transparent about the financial impact of the legislation on the customers if it is enacted in its current form. CNBC also reported that Amazon has said that thousands of customers contacted City Council members within hours of the campaign’s launch.The Delivery Protection Act, also known as Intro 518, is a proposed law aimed at changing how large delivery companies operate in New York City. The legislation, sponsored by City Council member Tiffany Cabán and backed by Mamdani, would introduce licensing requirements for last-mile delivery facilities and establish new worker safety, training and employment standards.It would also require companies operating these facilities, including Amazon, to directly employ workers involved in core delivery and warehouse services instead of relying on third-party contractors.Mamdani announced his support for the legislation in August, saying: “It's time to end the subcontracting model that puts profits over people and build an economy that works for working New Yorkers.”Mamdani quickly responded to Amazon's campaign on social media, accusing the company of attempting to shift responsibility for potential price increases onto city lawmakers. “Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed,” the mayor wrote on X, while urging lawmakers to pass the Delivery Protection Act.The dispute is the latest chapter in a broader battle between Mamdani and Amazon. Earlier this year, the mayor highlighted the collection of millions of dollars in idling fines from Amazon delivery vehicles and announced enforcement actions against retailers accused of selling illegal e-bikes, including products listed on Amazon, according to the WSJ report.New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin also criticised Amazon's campaign, calling the company's warnings misleading. Menin said the council is working on legislation that would regulate Amazon and strengthen worker protections without increasing costs for consumers or reducing jobs. The public clash comes just ahead of the holiday shopping season and Black Friday, one of Amazon's busiest sales periods, raising the stakes in the fight over how delivery workers should be employed and protected in New York City.
Article Summary: Amazon has launched an unusual in-app website campaign against New York City shoppers. Message warns that a proposed law backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani could lead to an increase in delivery costs by as much as $5 per order. Amazon redirects customers to a form which enables them to send pre-written emails to their City Council representatives opposing the measure.

Article Title: Apple plans iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, new MacBook Neo and entry-level iPad for February-March 2027
Article Text:
Apple's budget lineup arrives first in 2027

Apple's affordable devices get the first slot in 2027

The iPhone Air 2 and new iPads will follow soon after

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Apple's first big product wave of 2027 will start at the affordable end. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the iPhone 18e, a new entry-level iPad and the second-generation MacBook Neo are planned for February or March next year, with the standard iPhone 18 and a refreshed MacBook Air expected in the same window.In his latest Power On newsletter, Gurman said these devices are tied to Apple's iOS 27.4 release cycle, which runs across those two months. The higher-end models will arrive a little after that.The MacBook Neo, Apple's most affordable laptop, is now on a yearly update cycle, like the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. The new Neo, code-named J701, is mainly about the chip. Gurman said it moves from the A18 Pro to the A19 Pro, bringing 12GB of memory, faster performance and better graphics. Apple wants the Neo to take on entry-level Windows laptops and Chromebooks, and plans to refresh its colours often. First-generation owners, though, have little reason to upgrade.Earlier reports suggest the iPhone 18e and iPhone 18 will run on the A20 chip with 9GB of RAM and longer battery life. The entry-level iPad is tipped to get the A19 chip, which would finally bring Apple Intelligence to the cheapest iPad. It may also pack Apple's N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and the in-house C1X modem on cellular models.The MacBook Air is expected to move to the M6 chip.The iPhone Air 2, an OLED iPad Air and a refreshed iPad Pro are also lined up for the first half of 2027. Gurman said they sit slightly behind the budget models on Apple's manufacturing schedule, so a late March or April reveal looks likely.The iPhone Air 2 could add an ultra-wide camera, a smaller Dynamic Island and Apple's C2 modem with mmWave support in the US. The iPad Air is said to get an M5 chip and an OLED display in a thinner, lighter body. The iPad Pro may pick up an M6 or M7 chip along with vapour chamber cooling.Gurman expects Apple to split these reveals across multiple events, as it did with the iPhone Duo, HomeView and new Macs this year. Later in 2027, Apple is expected to bring a new Apple Watch, iPhone 20, smart glasses and AirPods with cameras.
Article Summary: Apple's first big product wave of 2027 will start at the affordable end. The iPhone 18e, a new entry-level iPad and the second-generation MacBook Neo are planned for February or March next year. Later in 2027, Apple is expected to bring a new Apple Watch, iPhone 20, smart glasses and AirPods.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says, ‘What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to…’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

'What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to mathematicians and programmers'

AI lowers barriers to specialised work

Agreeing with a professor’s essay

Read Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here

"The intellectual class never quite experienced the loss of purpose in their lives that many other classes of humans experienced. And this explains the heightened written angst.."

I agree with Prof Subbarao, who has done a lot of work in evaluating AI capability.

Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour (while I was on the road) that would have easily taken a very smart programmer at least a month to do.

It was not an easy piece of code at all and AI understood my high level intent very clearly and came up with a detailed plan and cleanly executed it and tested it against very detailed and exhaustive test cases it had constructed itself.

The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens.

And also yesterday, one of my non-technical colleagues showed me how he used his personal AI account to do the detailed mechanical CAD design for a motor housing, and the AI used a newly released low cost CAD software he had in his machine, which I doubt the AI was trained on.

He has no engineering background, but has a curious and active mind.

What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers and ...

On the positive side, the example of my non-technical colleague shows how AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI.

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution, warning that AI beginning to transform professions once considered safe from automation. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Vembu wrote that recent advances in AI have demonstrated capabilities which can dramatically reduce the time and expertise needed for tasks ranging from software development to engineering design. He also emphasised that the disruption is now reaching programmers, mathematicians and other intellectual professions mirrors what farmers, weavers, carpenters and ironsmiths experienced during earlier waves of industrialisation.Vembu said he recently used AI to optimise a complex piece of software code while travelling, a task he believes would have taken a highly skilled programmer at least a month to complete. "Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour," he wrote. According to Vembu, the AI not only understood the intended objective but also created a detailed execution plan, implemented the changes and generated extensive test cases on its own."The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens," he added.He also described how a non-technical colleague used a personal AI account to create a mechanical CAD design for a motor housing using newly released software, despite having no engineering background. Based on such experiences, Vembu concluded that AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. "What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers," he said.While highlighting the potential disruption, Vembu also pointed to what he sees as AI's democratising effect. He said his colleague's ability to perform engineering-related design work without formal training demonstrates how AI can empower people with curiosity and initiative to explore domains that were previously inaccessible."AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI," Vembu wrote. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities in coding, mathematics, scientific research and engineering, fuelling debate over their impact on jobs and professional expertise.Vembu said he agreed with Prof Subbarao, whom he credited with extensive work evaluating AI capability, and reacted to the professor’s essay on whether AI is destroying humanity’s sense of purpose. That essay, part of a “Sunday Harangue” series, argues that every technological revolution destroys purpose for some group, as industrialization did for weavers and craftsmen. What may be different this time, it says, is the class of people affected. Intellectuals have rarely faced such a loss, and they are articulate about it, which would explain the heightened angst.The essay says mathematicians may be conflating the loss of purpose in their own lives with a loss of purpose for humanity. A weaver could rightly say finished cloth is only a fraction of the experience of making it, it notes, yet most people welcome cheap machine-made cloth and civilization advanced. Civilization, it suggests, may not end because humans are not the only ones doing math. It adds that the angst does not pass down generations. The children of displaced weavers found purpose native to the new world. The loss is real but “generation-bounded,” the essay argues, which underlies its optimism that humanity, if not every individual, finds “a new equation” after the dip.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution. He said AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities.

Article Title: Delta system outage: Around 2000 flights delayed after technical glitch, what airline said after fixing issue
Article Text:
Delta Airlines outage

FAA also pauses few flights

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

About 2,000 Delta Air Lines flights across the US were delayed after a technical problem knocked out the automated system the carrier uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance before takeoff. By afternoon of November 22, Delta announced that the issue had been fixed and its automated calculations were back to normal operation, confirming that the outage was not caused by a computer hack. For much of the day, however, staff had to rely on manual workarounds to get planes off the ground safely, leaving roughly 49% of all Delta flights delayed.As per a report by The Associated Press, the airlines said that flights travelling to and from Atlanta were delayed after a computer system that works out how much an aircraft weighs stopped working. About 3% of its flights were cancelled.“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism,” the airline said in an earlier statement on Sunday.At the Atlanta airport, FlightAware said about 58% of departing flights and about 50% of arriving flights were delayed.Delta runs most of the flights from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. The airline said about 70% of the delays and cancellations FlightAware counted came from the automation fault, and the rest came from bad weather.According to a report by ABC News, to help stranded or delayed passengers, Delta said it is rebooking travelers onto the next best available itinerary while providing meals and hotel accommodations where necessary. For passengers whose flights were canceled and who choose not to travel, the airline confirmed that full refunds are being issued.Meanwhile, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also paused some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Delta’s hub, for about an hour. The FAA said on X that the delays were not linked to its air traffic systems. The FAA clarified that the disruption stemmed strictly from Delta's internal automation.“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information,” the FAA said.The latest outage arrives as millions of travelers prepare to fly this week for the Thanksgiving holiday. It also follows a turbulent stretch for US aviation, coming just days after an equipment installation problem triggered telecom issues and forced the FAA to issue only its second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks, which canceled thousands of flights and was followed by a separate United Airlines technical problem.
Article Summary: About 2,000 Delta Air Lines flights across the US were delayed after a technical problem knocked out the automated system the carrier uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance before takeoff. By afternoon of November 22, Delta announced that the issue had been fixed and its automated calculations were back to normal operation. About 3% of its flights were cancelled.

Article Title: Microsoft President Brad Smith on recent global outage: It was basically a perfect storm of ...
Article Text:
“It was basically a perfect storm of software that was updated four months earlier, and then it interacted with a new update and a shift in network traffic.”

“for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks.”

Read Brad Smith’s full explanation on the Microsoft outage

“Well, the first thing we always need to do when this happens is apologize, and we have, and I want to do so again. And you're right; it was not linked to AI. It wasn't a cyberattack. It was basically a perfect storm of software that was updated four months earlier, and then it interacted with a new update and a shift in network traffic. You know, we have taken steps.

We've published two reports in the last 10 days. We've worked to be transparent, showing minute by minute to the public what happened.

We've taken nine steps already, as we laid out in our report. There's 13 more steps we're going to take. We've learned a lot. It was painful, especially for everybody who relies on us. We get it, and I think this combination is going to make us stronger going forward. It's just constantly what we have to do in an age of such complex technology.”

“I think that is part of the really important question, and you can think about what's happening with all of these outages, at least in substantial part, as sort of AI ripple effects. What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you're a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

So what happened is we've set off, in effect, a race. Around the world, people who have technology are using these systems to identify the vulnerabilities and patch at a pace we have never seen before, to beat the bad actors so they can't use them to hack in, but especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you're trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can't take as much time to test what you're changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong, and that's what we've seen over the last week.

“Well, what I would say for all of us is three things. First, if you get an update on your phone or your laptop with a patch, apply it because I think that's going to keep your technology far safer. Second, for all the organizations in the world, people are having to update their patching practices. They're having to change the way their IT teams work together, they're having to upgrade their- their legacy infrastructure, and I think there's a huge opportunity for the government and the tech sector to work more closely together.

Jay Clayton is really, I think, focused on advancing this in the administration. I think that's critical, and we're going to need better sharing of threat intelligence, better concerted action.”

Microsoft President Brad Smith has explained what was behind the recent global outage. The disruption began on November 12 and lasted nearly 24 hours, leaving many Microsoft 365 customers unable to open their Outlook mailboxes or send and receive email. Some features in Teams and Copilot were also affected. Smith apologised to customers in a November 22 interview on CBS’s Face the Nation. Article Title: Mozilla to Apple: Why should we have to build Firefox twice for the iPhone
Article Text:
Why the browser engine matters

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What Apple’s browser choice screen can change

Mozilla has claimed that it would need to build Firefox twice. The browser maker says Apple ’s rules prevent it from bringing Gecko, the engine that powers Firefox on desktop and Android, to iPhone users through an update to the Firefox app they already have. The iPhone app currently uses WebKit, the same engine Apple uses in Safari.In a recent blog post, Mozilla said it would have to release Gecko in “a whole separate app, a second Firefox.” Existing users would then have to download that app, transfer their bookmarks, saved passwords and browsing history, and manually switch to it. Mozilla says those steps could deter people who already picked Firefox, including users who selected it from Apple’s browser choice screen in the European Union.A browser engine interprets a website’s code, draws the page on screen and runs scripts that make it interactive. Firefox on the iPhone has its own interface and account features, but WebKit handles the pages users open. On Windows, macOS and Android, Gecko does that work. Mozilla says some Firefox features are built into Gecko, which limits what it can bring to the iPhone while the app relies on WebKit.In 2024, Apple started allowing alternative engines in the EU under the Digital Markets Act, and soon thereafter, similar permissions were introduced in Japan with iOS 26.2.To use their own engine, developers need to get Apple’s approval. Apple says the terms are meant to protect users’ security and privacy, and developers have to promise to deliver timely security fixes. Its developer documentation also encourages breaking out things like page rendering and network traffic into their own components.In its March 2026 compliance report, Apple said browser makers can replace the WebKit version listed on the EU choice screen with a version that uses a different engine. That would let someone choosing Firefox from the screen download the Gecko app. Mozilla’s complaint concerns people who already have Firefox installed and would have to move to the new app themselves.Mozilla says millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iPhones has doubled since the EU began requiring Apple to offer a browser choice. The company says it has spent nearly three years testing Apple’s conditions and seeking changes. As of November 20, Mozilla said no developer had launched a non-WebKit browser under the rules in either the EU or Japan.
Article Summary: Mozilla says Apple’s rules prevent it from bringing Gecko, the engine that powers Firefox on desktop and Android, to iPhone users. The iPhone app currently uses WebKit, the same engine Apple uses in Safari. Existing users would have to download that app, transfer their bookmarks, saved passwords and browsing history, and manually switch to it.

Article Title: Oracle has a message for those who think it can't pay for its $300 billion OpenAI deal: With our final capital raise earlier this month, we became the first...

Oracle says it has every dollar it needs to deliver on its roughly $300 billion OpenAI contract. In a statement posted on November 20, shortly after US markets closed, the company said its final capital raise earlier this month made it the first hyperscaler fully funded for the current AI investment cycle. The financing it laid out at its Investor Day, including vendor financing, is now in place, Oracle added.The statement came at the end of a rough week for the stock. Oracle shares closed Friday at about $101, down more than 8% for the day and 19% for the week, closing out a seventh straight losing session. The stock now sits close to 70% below its record close from September 2025. Shares rose as much as 3.3% in after-hours trading after the statement went out.The raise Oracle is pointing to was worth $20 billion, split between about $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in debt.It also addressed its talks with suppliers. Any further private discussions with vendors "are just additional options," Oracle said, adding that its ability to deliver on the OpenAI contract does not depend on them.Investors have been asking how much money Oracle needs to build AI data centres and how much of its future rests on one customer.The OpenAI agreement runs over five years and makes up a large share of the company's $664 billion in remaining performance obligations. Earlier this month, Microsoft began winding down its own deal to rent AI computing from Oracle.Oracle paired the funding update with progress on the ground. Its Abilene, Texas campus, where OpenAI's Astra-6 model was trained, is nearly complete. Shackelford County, its next gigawatt-scale site, is fully permitted, and the handover of Nvidia Vera Rubin racks in its data halls is on track for the coming weeks.The two companies plan to add 4.5 gigawatts of US data centre capacity on top of the original Stargate site in Abilene.On the money side, Oracle stuck to its guidance. It expects positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 and is targeting more than $30 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2029. From that year, the company expects to fund its own growth.Oracle also said it stands by its funding position. "Any media reports that will come out and say the contrary are incorrect and wrong," the company said.

Why current AI flaws do not reassure former Google, Microsoft engineer

A former Google AI expert is so convinced that artificial intelligence (AI) will wipe out humanity that he stopped putting money into his retirement fund a decade ago. Machine learning researcher Nate Soares, who previously worked as a software engineer at both Google and Microsoft, recently shared the grim outlook during a recent podcast interview with The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson. According to Soares, there is a greater than 50% chance that AI will cause human extinction within the next 10 years.“I do not save for retirement now. I have a 401K from when I worked at Google, but I haven’t contributed to it for like a decade,” Soares said on the podcast. His comments came about two months after three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic claimed that AI could kill off humanity within the decade. Jacob Coxon resigned from his job in protest claiming Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI , were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat.Despite his bleak forecast, Soares said he does not believe human extinction is inevitable, and he spends his time doing everything he can to prevent it. Soares now serves as president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, a Berkeley-based nonprofit known for “AI doomerism”. He compared the daily reality of worrying about AI to how people have historically coped with the threat of nuclear annihilation.“It’s maybe the first time that we lived under the shadow of every human dying at once, but personally, we’ve always lived under the shadow of plague, shadow of war. And what you do is you do what you can and then you live a good life,” Soares said.During the interview, Thompson pushed back on the doomsday scenario, pointing out that even the most advanced AI systems today still run into plenty of bumps and limitations. Soares brushed off that reassurance, comparing the current state of AI to the early days of the automobile.“You could imagine a lot of horses looking at the development of the car and saying, 'Well, there’s all these things the car can’t do yet’. We are seeing AIs get better and better at things. We’re seeing them able to take on longer and longer tasks,” Soares told Thompson, as per New York Post.When it comes to the economy, Soares also made it clear he isn't worried about mass unemployment.“I’m not an 'AI jobs apocalypse guy’. I’m an 'AI kills all humans' guy, in which case you’ll be at full employment actually. We’ll be at full employment the moment before we’re all killed off,” he said.

Article Title: Back to work after Diwali? 7 ways ChatGPT can help you clear your inbox, organise tasks and catch up on pending projects
Article Text:
ChatGPT

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Returning to work after Diwali can mean more than just getting back to your routine. An overflowing inbox, pending approvals, back-to-back meetings and unfinished projects can make the first few days particularly hectic. With several tasks competing for attention, figuring out where to start can be a challenge. ChatGPT can help make the transition easier by summarising work updates, prioritising pending tasks, organising schedules and picking up projects left unfinished before the festive break. Here are seven ways to use ChatGPT to make your post-Diwali return to work less overwhelming.1. First things first: What did you miss while you were away?Before replying to the first email in your inbox, it helps to understand what actually happened while you were gone. With ChatGPT's app plugins, you can bring together relevant emails, documents and project updates to understand what's changed. Instead of working through individual threads, ask for a briefing organised by project, with the important decisions, outstanding requests and deadlines highlighted.Try asking: "I've been away for the Diwali break from [date] to [date]. Go through my work emails and relevant project documents from the past week.Tell me what changed while I was away, which decisions were made, what needs my response and which deadlines are coming up. Organise it by project and keep it concise."2. Everything looks urgent. But what actually needs to get done today?Once you've caught up, the next challenge is deciding what deserves your attention. There's a presentation due tomorrow, a colleague waiting for an approval, a report due Friday, and three requests marked urgent. They can't all be first on the list. Use ChatGPT to weigh deadlines, dependencies and impact, rather than just sorting tasks by when they arrived.Try asking: "Here's my list of pending work and deadlines. Help me prioritise it based on urgency, impact and whether someone else is waiting on my response to proceed. Identify the urgent things I should finish today, what I can schedule for later this week and anything that needs clarification before I begin."3. Your calendar has other plans for your week back.Just as you've figured out your priorities, you notice the back-to-back meetings on your calendar. There's barely an hour to get through the work you've just identified, let alone prepare for the discussions. You can review upcoming meetings alongside your priorities and find available time to focus. ChatGPT can also help you prepare for important conversations by pulling together the relevant context and suggesting questions or talking points.Try asking: "Look at my calendar for the next week and the priorities I've identified. Help me find realistic time to complete them, flag meetings I need to prepare for and suggest a plan that leaves room for unexpected requests."4. That half-finished presentation waiting for vendor inputs isn't going to finish itself.There was a proposal that was almost ready, a presentation waiting for final numbers or a project that needed one last round of feedback before the holidays. Returning to it now can mean spending an hour simply remembering what you'd already done.This is where Projects in ChatGPT can be useful. Keep related chats, reference files and project instructions together so you can return to the same body of work without reconstructing the context each time. You can ask ChatGPT to review earlier drafts, identify what's changed from conversations through the week and update the placeholders.Try asking: "I'm picking up this presentation after the festive break. Review the earlier draft, feedback and reference documents in this Project. Tell me what's complete, what's missing, look through vendor responses and update the placeholders. Help me work through the remaining sections one by one without changing the parts we've already finalized."5. For the approvals, reminders and conversations that went quiet.By this point, you've probably found a few loose ends. A vendor was meant to send revised costs, a colleague hasn't reviewed a document, and a client is waiting for a response. None is particularly difficult on its own, but together they can consume a surprising part of the day. You can work across apps to review relevant conversations and prepare context-specific follow-ups. Rather than sending a generic reminder, ChatGPT can help identify what was last agreed, what's outstanding and what the other person needs to do next.Try asking: "Review the conversations related to these three projects. Identify any pending approvals, unanswered questions or promised updates. Draft a short follow-up for each, referencing the last discussion and making the next action clear."6. The work is moving again. Can you make the next few days easier?A common problem with returning from a break is that the first day gets spent catching up while the work across projects continues to proceed. To be on top of it all. ChatGPT can help with scheduled reminders and recurring check-ins. Set a recurring reminder to revisit an outstanding approval or schedule a daily prompt to review priorities, so that important next steps don't disappear beneath new requests.Try asking: "Remind me tomorrow morning to check whether the proposal has been approved, set an 8 AM update on open and moving items across projects and at 9 AM, draft a list of closures for me to review my top work priorities for the day."7. Finally, find your rhythm without trying to finish the entire week today.You've caught up on what happened, identified the urgent work, and put a few things back in motion. But after the festivities, getting back into the rhythm of work can still take a little effort.This is where ChatGPT Voice offers a different way to organise your thoughts. Rather than staring at another to-do list, talk through what's on your mind, the ideas you want to feed into a presentation and the brief you have to share with a vendor. ChatGPT can help build these out while you speak, so you have a working ground to play with.Try saying: “I have a presentation to finish and a brief to send to a vendor, but my thoughts are still all over the place after the Diwali break. Let me talk you through what I have in mind. Help me organise these ideas into a presentation outline and draft the vendor brief into a draft email as we go. Ask me questions where you need more detail, and help me refine both as I think of changes.”
Article Summary: ChatGPT can help make the transition easier by summarising work updates, prioritising pending tasks, organising schedules and picking up projects left unfinished before the festive break. Here are seven ways to use ChatGPT to make your post-Diwali return to work less overwhelming.

Anthropic launched its IPO this week, bringing the company’s market value to nearly $1.3 trillion by the end of its first day of trading. Article Title: Anthropic founder to join Michael Dell, who pledged $6.25 billion, in donating to Trump Accounts
Article Text:
Warming ties between Anthropic and the Trump administration

What are Trump Accounts and how much Dell CEO has pledged

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown plans to contribute to US President Donald Trump’s cradle-to-adulthood investment program, known as Trump Accounts, news agency Reuters reported citing a source familiar with the matter. The move places Brown among a growing list of wealthy donors, including Michael Dell, who previously pledged $6.25 billion, backing the federal initiative. The planned donation comes right on the heels of Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering, where the artificial intelligence (AI) company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option to purchase additional shares.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted at the contribution during an interview with CNBC on Friday (November 20), noting that an Anthropic founder would be donating to the initiative “over the next few weeks,” though he did not name Brown directly.Brown’s contribution marks the latest step in Anthropic’s broader push to mend fences with the White House. In the past, the AI developer and its CEO, Dario Amodei, have occasionally clashed with Trump and senior officials over AI policy. In recent months, however, both sides have shown clear signs of moving toward a smoother working relationship:Serving as Anthropic’s chief compute officer, Brown has stepped forward as a primary bridge to the administration, attending a US-hosted G20 technology event in August as well as the September rollout of a government AI tool.Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Trump stated that he has “a lot of respect” for Amodei, signaling a noticeable thaw in relations between the president and the AI giant.Designed to encourage investing and build financial literacy from childhood, the Trump Accounts program provides government-funded investment accounts worth $1,000 to US citizens born between 2025 and 2028.Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell, are now the single largest private backers of Trump Accounts, the new US government investment accounts for children. Their $6.25 billion pledge puts $250 into the accounts of 25 million American kids aged 10 and under, and the couple said earlier this month that the full amount would be deposited within days.It is the biggest gift the Dells have ever made, more than double what their foundation gave away in its first 26 years. Most of their giving before this stayed in Texas, where Michael Dell started his company from a University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin) dorm room in 1984. In April, the couple became the first donors to cross $1 billion in lifetime giving to the university, with a $750 million commitment for a new medical campus.
Article Summary: Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown plans to contribute to US President Donald Trump’s cradle-to-adulthood investment program. The move places Brown among a growing list of wealthy donors, including Michael Dell, who previously pledged $6.25 billion, backing the federal initiative.

Article Title: As NASA's Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman says: Built with 1970s tech, still calling …
Article Text:
PC: NASA Science

What is NASA's Voyager 1

NASA's Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth

Milestones, challenges

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman praised NASA ’s Voyager 1 mission after the space agency announced that the spacecraft has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, nearly 49 years after its launch. Sharing his response, Mustafa Suleyman wrote on X (formerly Twitter), “This is incredible. Voyager 1 is now one single light-day from Earth: 16.1 billion miles, after 49 years of travel.” Adding further, he said: “Built with 1970s tech, still calling home. Patience is everything.” National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) shared a press release revealing that Voyager 1 is now around 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometres) from Earth, meaning signals travelling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and another 24 hours to return.NASA's Voyager 1 is a deep-space probe launched on September 5, 1977, that is the farthest human-made object from Earth and the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere, the boundary where the influences from outside our solar system are stronger than those from our Sun.It is also the first human-made object to venture into interstellar space. Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis.At Saturn, Voyager 1 found five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.Announcing the milestone via a press release, NASA said:NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun. ”Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger. ”In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space. On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth.Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question. ”Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world.“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars. ”
Article Summary: NASA's Voyager 1 is a deep-space probe launched on September 5, 1977. It is the farthest human-made object from Earth and the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis.

Article Title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has a message for Americans opposing data centres: Any scenario where the United States stops and...
Article Text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy

Amazon plans to spend around $220 billion on AI infrastructure this year

Voters and newly elected Democrats want new data centre projects paused

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said it would be a "historic mistake" for the US to pull back on building AI data centres, just weeks after a midterm election in which voters turned against the facilities in large numbers. Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event, Jassy argued that slowing down now would hand China the chance to set the rules for artificial intelligence."I cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centres and allows another country like China to establish all the norms," Jassy said, as reported by Semafor. He added that the US would regret such a move "for a very long time."Jassy did not brush the backlash aside, though. He acknowledged that tech companies need to "do it better and partner more closely with our communities."Few executives have more riding on the AI buildout than Jassy, who has directed hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres around the world. He reaffirmed that Amazon's capital expenditure will be around $220 billion this year and "meaningfully more" next year. He did not share a figure for 2027.In a TV interview after the event, Jassy went a step further. He said it would be a "catastrophic" mistake for the US to fall significantly behind China, and that the country had underinvested in its power grid even before AI came along.He compared the current buildout to the highways and bridges the US built in the 1950s.The White House is making a similar China argument. On Friday, President Donald Trump threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies that build AI data centres outside the country. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," he told reporters, adding that the US could fall behind China if the backlash slows construction at home. Trump said he had not yet told his staff about the plan, and it is not clear how it would be enforced. His advice to wary communities was to negotiate with tech companies for tax breaks, lower utility bills and direct payments. "Make them pay you. Make them pay your community," he said.Amazon is also bringing in outside money for some of its facilities. Blackstone's data centre trust has agreed to buy a 75% stake in two joint ventures that hold 13 AWS buildings, in a deal valued at about $5 billion.The backlash Jassy and Trump are responding to was one of the defining issues of this month's midterms. Democrats swept the elections, and voters rejected data centre development in nearly all of 41 local ballot measures. In one post-election voter poll, 56% of voters said AI and data centres were a crucial or major factor in how they voted.Several winning Democrats made data centres part of their victory speeches. "I do not work for data centres," Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown told supporters. Senator Bernie Sanders has since called for a national data centre moratorium.The pressure is building at the state level too. Incoming Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa has pledged to halt new data centre approvals until the state passes laws to protect residents. Texas alone is home to 27% of planned data centre capacity in the US, according to Wells Fargo.Public opinion was shifting well before the vote. A Pew Research Center survey conducted between July and August found that 54% of Americans think data centres are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half said they are mostly bad for home energy costs, while 60% said they would be uncomfortable with a new data centre operating in their area.Electricity bills are a big part of that worry. In a separate survey by researchers at Yale and George Mason University, 59% of Americans said they expect their power bills to go up if a data centre opens nearby. Only 15% said they would support one being built in their local area, while 56% said they would oppose it.
Article Summary: Voters and newly elected Democrats want new data centre projects paused. Jassy argued that slowing down now would hand China the chance to set the rules for artificial intelligence. He reaffirmed that Amazon's capital expenditure will be around $220 billion this year.

Article Title: Why Canadian billionaire Kevin O’Leary thinks Anthropic could be the next Amazon
Article Text:
Kevin O’Leary

Kevin O’Leary calls Anthropic’s AI approach ‘sheer genius’

Why Kevin O’Leary compares Anthropic to Amazon

The record breaking IPO of Anthropic

Amazon’s stake in Anthropic: Almost 15% stake worth around $225 billion

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Google’s stake in Anthropic: Around 13.7% stake worth nearly $200 billion

AI giant Anthropic has found a powerful supporter in Canadian billionaire and Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, who feels that the company’s enterprise-focused strategy could put it on a growth trajectory similar to that of Amazon . The comments from O’Leary came as Anthropic made its blockbuster Nasdaq debut, raising a record $81.3 billion and achieving a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, making it one of the most closely watched AI companies on Wall Street. In a post shared on social media platform X on the day Anthropic began trading, O’Leary called the company’s strategy “sheer genius.” He argued that it has spotted something other AI players have overlooked: business customers will pay a premium for technology they can trust and keep secure.O’Leary praised Anthropic’s focus on enterprise customers, and emphasised that the company has identified a key opportunity that many competitors have overlooked. As per the Shark Tank judge, businesses are ready to pay more on AI products that prioritise factors like trust, reliability and security. “Enterprise customers are willing to pay a premium for safety, security, and trust,” O’Leary wrote, describing Anthropic’s strategy as “sheer genius. ”The investor further added that strategy could help Anthropic in building a durable competitive advantage in the rapidly growing AI market, where enterprises are opting for secure solutions which can be deployed across critical business operations.O’Leary drew parallels between Anthropic and Amazon, noting that exceptional growth can justify massive valuations even before a company reaches consistent profitability. He argued that Anthropic’s current expansion resembles Amazon’s early growth story, although he believes the AI company is advancing at a significantly faster pace. The comparison reflects growing investor optimism around AI firms that are rapidly scaling revenue while securing large corporate customers.Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78. The offering raised $81.3 billion, the largest on record, and values the company at about $1.5 trillion. Shares opened at $111.50 and rose to nearly $115. They closed 17.07% above the IPO price, then slipped 4.70% in after-hours trading. About 832 million shares changed hands, more than SpaceX’s first-day volume, making Anthropic the most actively traded stock on the Nasdaq.Amazon and Google parent Alphabet are major investors. After the IPO, Amazon will reportedly hold 14.7% and Alphabet 13.7%, with Alphabet’s stake including $10 billion of shares bought in a private placement alongside the offering. Both companies also supply computing and other infrastructure to Anthropic.Amazon has been one of Anthropic's biggest strategic partners since the AI company began building its Claude models. Apart from investing in Anthropic, Amazon has also supplied much of the computing infrastructure needed to develop and run its AI models. Amazon first invested in Anthropic in 2023. According to the company's IPO-related filing, Amazon now holds around 14.7% of Anthropic's total equity. At the $83 IPO price, this stake is worth approximately $225 billion.Amazon's investment also involves convertible notes, which can be converted into shares. If all these notes were converted without the ownership limit, Amazon's stake could rise to 23.8% of Anthropic.However, Amazon has chosen not to waive the ownership cap for the IPO. This means it will hold the smaller stake for now, while the remaining notes will be dealt with under the terms of the agreement.Alphabet-owned Google is another major beneficiary of Anthropic's public listing. The search giant owns around 13.7% of the AI company, a stake valued at approximately $200 billion at the $83 IPO price. Google's investment includes 135.1 million shares that it agreed to purchase for $10 billion through a private placement priced at the IPO rate.For Google, Anthropic represents both an investment in a fast-growing AI company and a major customer for its cloud and computing services. The value of its holding could also change as Anthropic shares move in the public market.
Article Summary: Kevin O’Leary calls Anthropic’s AI approach ‘sheer genius’ The comments came as Anthropic made its blockbuster Nasdaq debut, raising a record $81.3 billion and achieving a valuation of about $1.5 trillion. Amazon and Google parent Alphabet are major investors in Anthropic.

Article Title: Microsoft will shut down To Do in June 2027 and is asking some of its users to pick another app
Article Text:
Microsoft To Do users on personal accounts have until June 30, 2027, to find a new app

Planner gets To Do's work users, but not their tasks, offline access or list groups

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wunderlist users who moved to To Do in 2020 now have to move again

Microsoft is retiring its To Do app on June 30, 2027, and people using it with a personal Microsoft account get no replacement, even if they pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family. The shutdown covers To Do on Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web. Work and school users will be moved to Planner, but their existing tasks and lists will not migrate with them.Microsoft disclosed the change on November 18, at the end of a long Planner blog post published during its Ignite conference. Its support page gives personal users one line of advice: "Choose another task-management application that meets your needs."Work users can see their old To Do tasks inside Planner until the deadline. After that, access ends. Shared lists, their members and their permissions will not carry over. Microsoft has promised an export tool but has not shared instructions yet. It also warns that exported data may not import into Planner or any other app. Retiring the apps does not by itself delete user data.Planner also lacks several To Do features. Microsoft has no plans for native Planner apps on Windows or Mac, and the web and Teams versions don't offer the same offline access.Private tasks can't take file attachments for now, list groups have no equivalent, and there are no plans for printing or emailing a list. The old Tasks feature in classic Outlook, meanwhile, will keep working.The move folds To Do and Planner into one system tied to Copilot and AI agents. "As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do," the Planner team wrote. Howard Crow, Microsoft's director of product for agents and AI, said the company recognises the change will affect customers differently, "particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts."To Do grew out of Wunderlist, which Microsoft picked up in 2015 when it bought the Berlin startup 6Wunderkinder for a reported $100 million to $200 million. The Wunderlist team built To Do, and Microsoft shut Wunderlist down in May 2020, moving its users over.Wunderlist founder Christian Reber, who now runs the rival app Superlist, replied on X: "I'd love to buy it back anytime!" Superlist already offers a To Do importer, and TickTick has posted a migration guide. Former Microsoft executive Brad Silverberg, who led Windows 95 development, said he has used To Do every day and is now looking at TickTick and Todoist.
Article Summary: Microsoft is retiring its To Do app on June 30, 2027. Work users can see their old To Do tasks inside Planner until the deadline. After that, access ends. Microsoft has no plans for native Planner apps on Windows or Mac.

Article Title: Google gives IIT Kharagpur $5 million to fund AI research and student training

Google has announced a $5 million (around Rs 46 crore) funding initiative for IIT Kharagpur aimed at advancing artificial intelligence research, expanding AI education programmes, and strengthening the institute's AI infrastructure. The announcement coincides with IIT Kharagpur's 75th anniversary celebrations and is intended to support the development of next-generation scientific and technical talent in India.According to Google, the funding will be channelled across three key areas: advanced AI research, educational opportunities, and AI capacity building. The initiative will support researchers and students working on AI applications in Indic languages, materials science, agriculture, and educational technology, with a focus on addressing real-world challenges through AI-driven solutions.As part of the education component, the programme will help expand AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty members, and teachers. Google said the effort is designed to broaden access to AI learning and equip future professionals with skills needed in an increasingly AI-driven economy.The third pillar of the partnership focuses on strengthening IIT Kharagpur's AI ecosystem through enhanced frameworks, tools, and infrastructure.The investment is expected to bolster the institute's technological capabilities and support AI innovation across the campus.Announcing the collaboration, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, an IIT Kharagpur alumnus, said the institute is already producing impactful work in fields such as Indic languages, agriculture, and education, and that Google is eager to accelerate this progress through the new partnership.He added that he looks forward to seeing the collaboration shape the next generation of students, much as IIT Kharagpur influenced his own journey.Speaking during the institute's 75th anniversary celebrations, IIT Kharagpur Director Suman Chakraborty said the support for applied AI research had been envisioned by Pichai. Article Title: ECB president Christine Lagarde predicts Europe is running short of data center capacity; warns about relying on foreign computing power, says: Should take first losses on …
Article Text:
Representative Image

“In technology, where projects such as chip plants and data centres need European scale, it means

public-private partnerships

at European level, with public money, including from the

EU budget

, taking the first losses and drawing in private capital,”

How much would it cost to expand Europe’s AI computing capacity

“But as long as we can buy computing power from foreign providers and frontier AI models remain available to us, the case for paying that price is hard to make,”

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why ECB president Christine Lagarde wants Europe to act early

ECB president Christine Lagarde has warned Europe about a lack of data center capacity. In a speech at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress this week, she called for the European Union to help finance chip plants and data centers. Lagarde said public funds should take on some of the financial risk to attract private investors to projects that need to be built at a European scale. Taking the first losses means public funds would absorb initial losses if a project underperformed. That would reduce how much private investors stand to lose and could make them more willing to fund costly projects.Lagarde said.Lagarde has previously warned that Europe lacks the data center capacity to meet its own demand and that plans for up to seven AI gigafactories in the EU fall short. In Frankfurt, she cited an estimate that raising Europe’s share of global AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030 would require about €1.3 trillion in investment.she added.Lagarde warned that relying on foreign technology can leave Europe vulnerable if that dependence is used as leverage. She said the difficulty for policymakers is building support for costly investments while businesses can still buy what they need from abroad.Lagarde pointed to the EU’s €800 billion pandemic recovery fund and its financial and geopolitical support for Ukraine as examples of the bloc acting when member states agreed on the need for a common response. She said it was harder to build that consensus around problems whose costs become apparent gradually.She cited the EU’s unfinished effort to integrate its capital markets as another example. Without a common capital market and supervisory system, she said, more European savings are invested abroad each year and more of the bloc’s growing companies look elsewhere for financing.
Article Summary: ECB president Christine Lagarde has warned Europe about a lack of data center capacity. She called for the European Union to help finance chip plants and data centers. Lagarde said public funds should take on some of the financial risk to attract private investors to projects that need to be built at a European scale.
